Getting into Yoga: What is it, what does it mean, and how to get into it. Yoga, an ancient practice that has been around for thousands of years, continues to gain popularity in today's fast-paced world. It's no surprise that more and more people are looking for ways to incorporate yoga into their daily lives. Yoga offers a wide range of benefits, from improved flexibility and strength to stress relief and mental clarity. If you're curious about starting your own yoga journey, this comprehensive guide will help you take your first steps. We'll explore the history and essence of yoga, learn how to find the right style and teacher, and share tips for getting started. Let's dive in! What is Yoga? Yoga is a holistic mind-body practice that originated in ancient India over 5,000 years ago. It is a discipline that encompasses physical, mental, and spiritual aspects. Yoga, derived from the Sanskrit word "yuj," means "to join" or "to unite." It is a practice that aims to connect the mind, body, and spirit to achieve a state of balance and harmony. Yoga involves a combination of physical postures (asanas), breath control (pranayama), and meditation (dhyana). These elements work together to promote overall well-being, improve mental and emotional health, and cultivate self-awareness. Regular practice of yoga can help individuals develop flexibility, strength, balance, and inner peace. The Different Styles of Yoga One of the fascinating aspects of yoga is its diversity. There are several different styles of yoga, each with its unique approach and focus. Some of the more popular styles include: - Hatha Yoga: This is a gentle, slow-paced style that emphasizes basic postures and breathing techniques. Hatha yoga is ideal for beginners and those looking for a more relaxed practice. - Vinyasa Yoga: A dynamic and flowing style, Vinyasa yoga links breath and movement, creating a dance-like sequence of postures. This style is suitable for those who enjoy a more active practice and want to build strength and flexibility. - Ashtanga Yoga: This is a rigorous, structured practice that involves a specific sequence of postures performed in a continuous flow. Ashtanga yoga is ideal for those seeking a challenging, disciplined practice that promotes strength and stamina. - Iyengar Yoga: This style focuses on alignment and precision, using props such as blocks, straps, and bolsters to support the body in various postures. Iyengar yoga is suitable for those looking to improve their posture and flexibility while minimizing the risk of injury. - Yin Yoga: A slow, meditative practice, Yin yoga targets the deep connective tissues and fascia in the body. It involves holding postures for extended periods, allowing for deep relaxation and stress relief. Finding the Right Yoga Teacher. A great yoga teacher can make all the difference in your yoga journey. They can guide you through the practice, help you avoid injuries, and inspire you to grow both on and off the mat. Here are some tips for finding the right yoga teacher for you: - Look for a certified teacher: Check if the teacher has completed a yoga teacher training program accredited by a reputable organization such as Yoga Alliance. This ensures that they have the necessary knowledge and skills to teach safely and effectively. - Attend different classes: Try out various classes and teachers to find the one that resonates with you. Each teacher has their unique teaching style, and it's essential to find someone you feel comfortable with and inspired by. - Seek a balance of challenge and support: A good yoga teacher should challenge you to explore your limits while also providing support and encouragement. They should be able to adapt the practice to your individual needs, helping you progress at your own pace. - Prioritize clear communication: Effective communication is vital in a yoga class. Look for a teacher who can clearly explain the postures, provide modifications when needed, and offer feedback to help you improve your practice. - Consider their teaching philosophy: A yoga teacher's personal philosophy and approach to teaching can impact the overall class experience. Seek out a teacher whose values and intentions align with your own. Tips for Starting & Finding Your Yoga Practice Now that you have a better understanding of yoga and how to find the right teacher, it's time to get started. Before you begin - always consult your physician before beginning any exercise program. This general information is not intended to diagnose any medical condition or to replace your healthcare professional. Consult with your healthcare professional to design an appropriate exercise prescription that’s right for you. Here are some tips to help you embark on your yoga journey: - Start with the basics: Begin your practice with a beginner-friendly style like Hatha yoga to learn the fundamental postures and breathing techniques. This will provide a solid foundation for exploring other styles in the future. - Invest in a quality yoga mat: A good yoga mat is essential for a comfortable practice. Look for one that provides sufficient cushioning, has a non-slip surface, and is easy to clean. - Dress comfortably: Wear clothing that allows for freedom of movement and is made of breathable materials. Avoid wearing accessories like belts or jewelry that may interfere with your practice. - Practice regularly: Consistency is key in developing a successful yoga practice. Aim to practice at least 2-3 times per week to build strength, flexibility, and body awareness. - Listen to your body: Pay attention to your body's signals and avoid pushing yourself too hard, especially when you're just starting. Remember that progress takes time, and it's essential to be patient and kind to yourself. - Don't compare yourself to others: Yoga is a personal journey, and everyone's practice will look different. Focus on your own progress and avoid comparing yourself to others in the class. - Embrace the mental and spiritual aspects: While yoga is often associated with physical fitness, it's essential to remember that it's a holistic practice. Engage with the mental and spiritual aspects of yoga through meditation, breathwork, and self-reflection. Your Journey into Yoga Getting into yoga can be an incredibly rewarding experience that enriches your life on many levels. By understanding the essence of yoga, exploring different styles, finding the right teacher, and following the tips mentioned above, you'll be well on your way to a fulfilling yoga journey. Remember that yoga is not just about mastering the physical postures – it's about cultivating a deep connection between your mind, body, and spirit. So, take a deep breath, unroll your mat, and welcome the transformative power of yoga into your life.

How to start learning yoga As a beginner, you should build upon your practice slowly and really get to know each pose before learning a new one. As a yoga newbie, give yourself time to become familiar with the practice. Overstretching is a thing, and other injuries can happen from yoga. 10 yoga poses a beginner should learn first There are certain asanas (postures) that you will perform in almost every single yoga class so I recommend that you learn these poses first. These specific yoga postures should become like second nature to you, and you'll want to be able to recall them quickly from memory. Here are ten poses you should familiarize yourself with first when you start learning yoga: - Cat cow - Child's pose - Downward-facing dog - Upward-facing dog - Plank pose - Cobra pose - Warrior 1 - Warrior 2 - Chair pose - Low lunge 1. Cat cow Cat cow, also called Chakravakasana, is great for warming up your spine and activating your core. To perform the alternating sequence of cat-cow, begin on all fours with your shoulders stacked over your wrists and your hips stacked over your knees: - For cow: Inhale deeply while dropping your lower back towards the floor while keeping your abs engaged. Bring your head up and tilt your pelvis up and broaden your collarbones. - For cat: From cow, exhale deeply while pulling your navel in towards your spine and rounding your back to draw your shoulder blades apart. - Drop your head so that your gaze is towards your navel, and tuck your tailbone under. 2. Child's Pose Child's pose, also called Balasana, is a classic resting pose and a slignt hip opener. Here's how to do Child's Pose: - First come to your hands and knees, move your big toes towards one another to touching with the tops of your feet to the mat. - Take your knees hip distance apart. Sit back onto your heels. - Rest your forehead to the mat. - Bring your hands forward with your palms facing down or behind you with palms up. - Close your eyes and relax into the pose. 3. Downward-Facing Dog Down Dog, also called Adho Mukha Svanasana, is an inversion and one of the most commonly practiced yoga poses performed in nearly every yoga class. Here's how to do Downward Facing Dog: - From a tabletop position, using your core, draw your hips up to the sky and your chest towards the back of the mat into down dog. - Walk your feet back until you are in an inverted V position. - Root down through your feet and continue lifting from the core to lengthen your side body. Your hands should remain shoulder-distance apart, and your feet should remain hip-distance apart. Keep your ears in line with your arms to lengthen your neck. 4. Upward-Facing Dog Up Dog, also called Urdhva Mukha Svanasana) is a chest-opening pose and a beginner-friendly backend. Here's how to do Up Dog: - From a Cobra position, push firmly through your hands and the tops of your feet, and straighten your arms to lift your chest. Your shoulders, elbows, and wrists should be stacked. - Knit your shoulder blades together and down to draw the chest forward. - Broaden your collarbones. Keep your pelvis and knees lifted. - Gaze forward or up to lengthen the back of the neck. 5. Plank Pose Plank, also called Phalakasana, is another foundational pose, and it's great for building core strength. Here's how to do Plank pose: - From a Table Top position, place your hands on the mat beneath your shoulders. Spread your fingers wide with your middle fingers pointing forward. - Step back with your feet hip distance apart or with your feet together for more leg engagement. - Stack the balls of your feet beneath your heels. Straighten your legs by engaging your quadriceps to lift the kneecaps. - Gaze down to lengthen the back of the neck. 6. Cobra Pose Cobra, also called Bhujangasana, is a beginner-friendly backend that doesn't require the strength of Upward Facing Dog. Here's how to do Cobra: - Lie on the ground with your chest on the floor. Place your feet hip-distance apart. Bring your hands in line with your elbows and bottom ribs. - Straighten your legs by engaging your quadriceps and glutes. Press firmly through the tops of the feet to lift the kneecaps off the mat. - Lightly press through your hands. Knit your shoulder blades together and down to draw your chest forward and up. - Gaze forward to lengthen the back of the neck. 7. Warrior 1 Warrior 1, also called Virabhadrasana 1, is one of the first poses all yogis learn. It's a foundational standing posture. Here's how to do Warrior 1: - From Mountain Pose, step back with one foot. - Keep your feet hip distance apart to square your hips to the front of the mat. Stack your front shin in a straight line from knee to ankle. - Spin the back heel to the mat and angle the toes to point slightly forward and out. Root down through the feet and lift your back inner thigh to the sky. - Engage your core to lift the torso, and reach your arms to the sky with hands shoulder-distance apart. - Pull your legs energetically towards each other to find mula bandha. Gaze forward or up. 8. Warrior 2 Warrior 2, also called Virabhadrasana 2, is a very commonly performed posture that you'll practice in many different types of classes. Here's how to do Warrior 2: - From Warrior 1, maintain your stance and open your body to the side. - Change your back foot position to be in line with the back of your mat. The heel of your front foot should be in line with the arch of the back foot. - Bend your front knee directly over your ankle, bringing your front thigh parallel to the mat. To straighten the back leg, lift the inner thigh while opening the front hip. - Keeping your torso upright, engage the upper back. - Reach your arms out parallel to the mat, away from the body. Gaze forward. 9. Chair pose Chair, also called Utkatasana, is a basic standing pose that's great for improving leg strength. Here's how to do Chair Pose: - From Mountain Pose (Tadasana), bend your knees deeply and shift weight into your heels. - Try to bring your shins into a straight line from your knees to the tops of your feet. - Lift your arms to the sky with your palms facing one another and fingers spread wide. Gaze forward or up. 10. Low Lunge Low Lunge, also called Anjaneyasana, is a nice hip flexor stretch, and it's a great pose for improving your balance. Here's how to do Low Lunge: - From Mountain Pose, step back with one foot and place it on the ground behind you. Keep your feet hip-distance apart to square hips to the front of the mat. - Stack your front shin in a straight line from knee to ankle. Lower your back knee to the mat and untuck the toes. Reach your arms to the sky with hands shoulder distance apart. - Gaze forward or up. It can be fun and challenging for yoga instructors to teach people new to yoga. To help beginners take their first steps, you need a special set of skills and knowledge. The challenge for many yoga teachers is making yoga fun and easy for people just starting out. This article will discuss the art of teaching yoga to beginners and: - How teachers can enhance their skills by understanding the beginner’s mindset - How to structure an effective class, and share communication strategies that resonate with new students - Address common challenges yoga teachers face when working with beginners - Practical solutions to overcome them Understanding the Beginner’s Mindset It’s important for yoga teachers to fully understand beginners’ mindsets when teaching yoga. Understanding the common concerns and misconceptions that new students often carry to their first yoga class is essential. Many beginners are anxious about starting yoga because they believe they may not be fit or flexible enough to participate. It’s critical to address these issues and establish a welcoming environment that inspires students to embrace their journey, regardless of their current skill level. Common fears and misconceptions Misconceptions about yoga are common with new students and may slow their learning process. Some people think that yoga is just for those who are flexible or that they need to be in excellent physical shape to practice. Some people may believe yoga is overly spiritual or mystical. It is your responsibility as a yoga teacher to dispel these myths and help students understand that yoga is accessible to everyone, whatever their faith or physical condition. Emphasizing that yoga is a personal journey and that each person begins at their own unique time will help ease these fears. Students should be encouraged to focus on their accomplishments instead of comparing themselves with others. Remind them that with regular practice, both their strength and mobility will increase. Creating a welcoming environment A welcoming environment is essential for building confidence in new students. For new students to feel comfortable, the classroom needs to be a friendly place. When the students enter your class, greet each one by name. This small act shows that you appreciate them being there and gives them a chance to talk about any concerns or limitations they may have. Create a non-judgmental space where students feel safe to explore their practice. Use language that invites rather than demands, and remind students that they are their own best teachers. Encourage them to listen to their bodies and modify poses as needed. Ensure that your studio is equipped with props to accommodate various body types and physical limitations, making the practice more accessible to all. Building confidence in new students It’s important to give new students confidence so that they can keep practicing. Begin by telling them it’s okay to feel nervous; it shows that they care about their practice. Remind them that yoga isn’t about being perfect but about growing and learning about yourself. Give clear directions and examples, and break down poses into steps that are easy to follow. Provide modifications and encourage students to choose the variation that feels right for their bodies. Use positive reinforcement to acknowledge their efforts and progress, no matter how small. As a yoga teacher, your role is to empower students to develop their practice. Encourage them to ask questions and express their needs. You can help people who are new to yoga gain confidence and start a long-term yoga practice by creating a helpful space and addressing common worries and misconceptions. Structuring Your Beginner Yoga Class Structuring a beginner yoga class requires careful planning and consideration. A well-designed class helps new students feel comfortable and builds their confidence as they explore yoga. Let’s examine the main elements of a good beginning yoga class structure. Warm-up and breathing exercises Begin your class with gentle warm-up exercises and breathing techniques to prepare students’ bodies and minds for the practice. Start with simple movements to loosen up the joints and muscles. Incorporate basic pranayama exercises, such as deep belly breathing or alternate nostril breathing, to help students connect with their breath and focus their attention. As a yoga teacher, guide your students through these exercises slowly, providing clear instructions and demonstrations. Emphasize the importance of breath awareness throughout the class, as it helps to calm the mind and enhance the mind-body connection. Basic pose breakdowns When teaching yoga to beginners, introduce fundamental yoga poses, breaking them down into manageable steps. Provide detailed instructions on proper alignment and offer modifications for different body types and abilities. Demonstrate each pose and walk around the room to offer gentle adjustments and encouragement. Remember to use clear, simple language and avoid complex yoga terms that might confuse new students. Incorporating props effectively Props can be valuable tools in a beginner yoga class, making poses more accessible and helping students maintain proper alignment. Introduce common props such as blocks, bolsters, and blankets, explaining their purpose and demonstrating how to use them effectively. For example, blocks can provide support in standing poses or help students reach the floor in forward folds. Bolsters create relaxation and help soften postures. Blankets can offer comfort and support in seated poses or during relaxation. Encourage students to use props as needed, emphasizing that they are aids to enhance their practice, not crutches. Cool-down and relaxation techniques End your beginner yoga class with a proper cool-down and relaxation session. Include gentle poses and twists to release any tension. Gradually transition into more restorative poses, such as Legs-Up-the-Wall or Reclined Bound Angle Pose. End with Savasana (Corpse Pose), guiding students through a short relaxation or meditation. This last rest helps students take in the benefits of their practice and makes them feel calm and re-energized. As a yoga teacher, remember that structuring a beginner class is about creating a safe space where new students can explore yoga at their own pace. By incorporating these elements into your class structure, you’ll provide a solid foundation for beginners to develop their practice and experience the life-changing benefits of yoga. Effective Communication Strategies As a yoga teacher, the way you communicate instructions and give personalized feedback can have a significant impact on your student’s progress and experience. Let’s look at some important ways to improve how you talk to people in the yoga class. Clear and concise instructions When teaching yoga to beginners, it’s important to keep your cues simple. Focus on guiding students into the basic form of each pose, providing one or two additional alignment cues if needed. Don’t use complicated yoga terms that could be confusing. Instead, use language that non-yogis can easily understand. For example, when instructing students to move into Warrior II pose, provide clear directions on which way to face, how wide their stance should be, and where to place their hands and feet. If relevant, mention whether to enter the pose on an inhale or exhale. By using accessible language and breaking down poses into manageable steps, you’ll help beginners feel more comfortable and confident in their practice. Demonstrating poses Visual demonstrations are valuable tools for teaching yoga to beginners. When demonstrating a pose, make sure that all students can see you. Make eye contact with your students and look for signs of understanding. This connection helps create a supportive environment and allows you to gauge whether further explanation is needed. After the demonstration, summarize the key points of the pose, providing no more than three simple takeaways to help students perform it effectively. Offering modifications and variations Instead of using the term “modifications,” which may imply that a student isn’t doing “real” yoga, consider offering “variations” for all bodies and skill levels. This approach promotes inclusivity and empowers students to choose what feels best for their bodies at any given moment. Introduce props like blocks, bolsters, and blankets at the beginning of class, explaining how to use them effectively to support various poses. For example, when teaching a balance pose like Tree Pose, offer variations such as keeping both feet on the ground, placing the lifted foot on the ankle, or bringing it higher up the leg. Emphasize that all variations are equally valid expressions of the pose, encouraging students to listen to their bodies and choose the option that feels best for them. Providing personalized feedback Offering constructive feedback is important when teaching yoga to beginners. When giving feedback, ask if the student is open to receiving it. Frame your comments with the end in mind, emphasizing behavior that can be changed instead of generalizations. Use “I” messages, such as “I’ve noticed” or “I’m concerned about,” rather than “you” messages like “you always” or “you never.” Keep your emotions out of the feedback and remain respectful and objective. When possible, have private conversations for personalized feedback to avoid potential embarrassment in front of the class. Remember to speak clearly, demonstrate poses effectively, offer variations for all bodies, and provide thoughtful, personalized feedback to help your students thrive in their yoga journey. Addressing Common Challenges Teaching yoga to beginners comes with its own set of challenges. A yoga teacher should be prepared to handle various situations that may arise during classes. Let’s explore some common challenges and strategies and address them. Dealing with mixed-level classes One of the most frequent challenges yoga teachers face is managing a class with students of different skill levels. To create a supportive environment for all, start by teaching to the majority of the room. This means catering the level of instruction to about 80% of the students who are at a similar level. However, don’t ignore the remaining 20%. Offer modifications and variations to accommodate both beginners and more advanced practitioners. For example, when teaching a peak pose, have newer students work on repeating the preparatory poses to gain strength and endurance. Meanwhile, more experienced students can attempt the full expression of the pose. This way, everyone in the class feels challenged and supported. Managing time effectively Time management is crucial when teaching yoga to beginners. To keep your class on track, consider creating a notebook or binder with various sequences organized by asana categories. This will help you quickly adapt your class plan if needed. Set a timer for savasana to ensure you don’t run over your class time. Additionally, try to stack your classes back-to-back each day to maximize your teaching efficiency. This approach allows you to maintain a consistent flow and energy throughout your teaching schedule. Handling questions and concerns Beginners often have many questions about yoga practice. To address this, create a culture of safety in your class by encouraging students to approach you with their concerns. Before class, take the time to talk to your students and identify any potential issues or limitations they may have. If you’re unsure about how to address a specific concern, it’s okay to admit that you don’t know the answer. Offer to find out more information or direct the student to a qualified professional who can help. This honesty will build trust and respect between you and your students. Encouraging consistent practice Consistency is key to reaping the benefits of yoga. To motivate your students to maintain a regular practice, emphasize the importance of showing up on both easy and challenging days. Remind them that a consistent yoga practice helps calm the fluctuations of the mind and leads to personal growth. Consider using a habit-tracking app, journal, or wall calendar to help students visualize their progress. Encourage them to start with a simple practice, even if it’s just for a few minutes each day. This approach makes it easier for beginners to incorporate yoga into their daily routines and experience positive effects over time. Creating a Supportive Environment Teaching yoga to beginners requires patience, understanding, and a well-rounded approach. You now know how to grasp the beginner’s mindset, structure classes thoughtfully, communicate effectively, tackle common challenges, and create a supportive environment for newcomers to explore and grow. In the end, mastering the art of teaching yoga to beginners goes beyond just knowing the poses. It’s about creating a welcoming space where students feel safe to learn, make mistakes, and discover the transformative power of yoga. By implementing what you’ve learned, you can have a positive impact on your students’ confidence and motivation, laying the groundwork for a lifelong yoga practice. Remember, every expert was once a beginner, and your guidance as a teacher plays a crucial role in shaping their yoga journey. 8 Easy Tips for Yoga Beginners It may be an ancient practice, but the power of yoga only seems to grow stronger with time. The practice has become increasingly popular in recent years, with over 300 million people around the world adding a yoga workout to their wellness routines today. In fact, Americans alone spend over $16 billion on yoga classes and equipment every year! While it's a given that working with experienced yoga instructors and yoga teachers can help maximize results and improve one's physical and mental health, it is also important to experience the joy of yoga in a personal space and get in touch with ourselves! In this blog, we share a few tips for beginners who wish to start practicing yoga today. Tips for a healthy yoga practice - - Specify a proper time - Choose a comfortable place - Practice on a light stomach - Start off early - Be gentle - Set the mood - Try out different yoga poses - Be consistent Before you settle into a regular yoga practice, it would make a huge difference to your well-being if you got a hang of the best practices recommended above. So, let's deep dive into these tips for beginners and set you up for a truly healthy yoga routine! 1. Specify a proper time This may sound easy, but it's easy to slip out of a routine if you're not careful! It's also why people prefer joining a yoga class to help them establish a regular practice. The best time to bring out the yoga mat is just an hour after you wake up or in the evening. Warm up with your basic yoga poses before picking up a more advanced workout in your yoga classes. Yoga at these times can also be a good way to refresh the mind and release stress collected during the day. Fixing a time will get you in the habit of doing yoga exercises every day without fail. 2. Choose a comfortable place People recommend practicing yoga at your home. But if you are practicing at home, there are chances you might be faced with multiple distractions. Yoga calls for a consistent mind-body connection as you practice physical postures and breathing techniques and these exercises require focus and a relaxed state of mind. It would be ideal for your practice to choose a private corner for your yoga session at home where you will not be disturbed or come in the way of your family. Consider it your personal yoga studio and treat it like a true sanctuary! 3. Practice on a light stomach The next most important thing to keep in mind is that yoga postures are always best practiced on a light or empty stomach. You can practice yoga poses and meditate about 2-3 hours after your meal. 4. Start off easy As you are a beginner, it can be easy to get overwhelmed by the various disciplines like Vinyasa yoga, Hatha yoga, or Ashtanga yoga, among others. But to get started, it's best to go with easy-to-do yoga sequences and stretching exercises. Once you are able to master the basics on your own, you will be able to explore more advanced poses with a qualified yoga teacher who can guide you through the finer aspects of the practice. Even doing yoga for 20 minutes initially, including your basic breathing exercises, can go a long way in building your core. Stretching is needed to warm you up before doing intense yoga postures. This is an absolute must, else you may risk straining your muscles. 5. Be gentle Yoga may be a physical practice but the purpose is to be able to relax as you workout. Wear comfortable clothing and go through your exercises without rushing the flow. Take short breaks between each pose and enjoy your workout with a smile! 6. Set the mood Yoga is all about achieving mental clarity and finding inner peace. So, set the mood at home to support your mental well-being. You could dim the lights and play soft music in the background to help reduce stress and also keep you motivated as you practice. 7. Try out different Yoga postures After starting off as a novice try to train the different Yoga techniques to get more benefits. Some of them are as follows: Standing Sideways Bending One arm (Konasana) Sideways Bending Using Both arms (Konasana 2) Standing Spinal Twist (Katichakrasana) Standing Forward Bend (Hastapadasana) Standing Backward Bend (Ardha Chakrasana) Triangle Pose (Trikonasana) Warrior Pose (Veerabhadrasana or Virabhadrasana) Standing Forward Bend with Feet Apart (Parsarita Padotanasana) Tree Pose (Vrikshasana) Reverse Prayer Pose (Paschim Namaskarasana) Eagle Pose (Garudasana) Chair Pose (Utkatasana) One-Legged Forward Bend (Janu Shirasasana) Two-Legged Forward Bend (Paschimottanasana) Inclined Plane (Poorvottanasana) Side Plank Pose (Vasisthasana) Downward Facing Dog Pose (Adho Mukha Svanasana) Dolphin Plank Pose (Makara Adho Mukha Svanasana) Sitting Half Spinal Twist (Ardha Matsyendrasana) Butterfly Pose (Badhakonasana) Lotus Pose (Padmasana) One-Legged Pigeon Pose (Eka Pada Raja Kapotasana) Cat Stretch (Marjariasana) Camel Pose (Ustrasana) Child Pose (Shishuasana) Mill Churning Pose (Chakki Chalanasana) Bow Pose (Dhanurasana) Cobra Pose (Bhujangasana) Sphinx Pose (Salamba Bhujangasana) Superman Pose (Viparita Shalabhasana) Locust Pose (Shalabasana) Boat Pose (Naukasana) Bridge Pose (Setu Bandhasana) Fish Pose (Matsyasana) Wind-Relieving Pose (Pavanamuktasana) Shoulder Stand (Sarvangasana) Plow Pose (Halasana) Lying-down Body Twist (Natrajasana) Lying-down on sides (Vishnuasana) Corpse Pose (Shavasana) 8. Be consistent Whatever you have read about yoga till now is useless if you don't keep your practice going after the first few days. It is very important to be regular with your yoga practice. Try to make it a part of your daily schedule as then it would be easier to make it a habit. Beginners can learn yoga at home, but should take proper precautions and ease into it, just as you would ease into weight training. If you've never attended a yoga class and you're not familiar with the asanas of yoga, it's imperative that you start practicing beginner poses first. DoYogaWithMe is a great online yoga option for beginner yogis to learn yoga. They have a robust beginner section with a dedicated area called Basics For Beginners. This section contains beginner videos about breath and bandhas, alignment, stabilization, and core strength. All of which are critical components of a safe and effective yoga practice. How to start learning yoga As a beginner, you should build upon your practice slowly and really get to know each pose before learning a new one. In an ideal scenario, you complete an entire beginner series so you learn the foundational poses first, and then you add a new pose in each week. As a yoga newbie, give yourself time to become familiar with the practice. Overstretching is a thing, and other injuries can happen from yoga. 10 yoga poses a beginner should learn first There are certain asanas (postures) that you will perform in almost every single yoga class so I recommend that you learn these poses first. These specific yoga postures should become like second nature to you, and you'll want to be able to recall them quickly from memory. Here are ten poses you should familiarize yourself with first when you start learning yoga: - Cat cow - Child's pose - Downward-facing dog - Upward-facing dog - Plank pose - Cobra pose - Warrior 1 - Warrior 2 - Chair pose - Low lunge 1. Cat cow Cat cow, also called Chakravakasana, is great for warming up your spine and activating your core. To perform the alternating sequence of cat-cow, begin on all fours with your shoulders stacked over your wrists and your hips stacked over your knees: - For cow: Inhale deeply while dropping your lower back towards the floor while keeping your abs engaged. Bring your head up and tilt your pelvis up and broaden your collarbones. - For cat: From cow, exhale deeply while pulling your navel in towards your spine and rounding your back to draw your shoulder blades apart. - Drop your head so that your gaze is towards your navel, and tuck your tailbone under. 2. Child's Pose Child's pose, also called Balasana, is a classic resting pose and a slignt hip opener. Here's how to do Child's Pose: - First come to your hands and knees, move your big toes towards one another to touching with the tops of your feet to the mat. - Take your knees hip distance apart. Sit back onto your heels. - Rest your forehead to the mat. - Bring your hands forward with your palms facing down or behind you with palms up. - Close your eyes and relax into the pose. 3. Downward-Facing Dog Down Dog, also called Adho Mukha Svanasana, is an inversion and one of the most commonly practiced yoga poses performed in nearly every yoga class. Here's how to do Downward Facing Dog: - From a tabletop position, using your core, draw your hips up to the sky and your chest towards the back of the mat into down dog. - Walk your feet back until you are in an inverted V position. - Root down through your feet and continue lifting from the core to lengthen your side body. Your hands should remain shoulder-distance apart, and your feet should remain hip-distance apart. Keep your ears in line with your arms to lengthen your neck. 4. Upward-Facing Dog Up Dog, also called Urdhva Mukha Svanasana) is a chest-opening pose and a beginner-friendly backend. Here's how to do Up Dog: - From a Cobra position, push firmly through your hands and the tops of your feet, and straighten your arms to lift your chest. Your shoulders, elbows, and wrists should be stacked. - Knit your shoulder blades together and down to draw the chest forward. - Broaden your collarbones. Keep your pelvis and knees lifted. - Gaze forward or up to lengthen the back of the neck. 5. Plank Pose Plank, also called Phalakasana, is another foundational pose, and it's great for building core strength. Here's how to do Plank pose: - From a Table Top position, place your hands on the mat beneath your shoulders. Spread your fingers wide with your middle fingers pointing forward. - Step back with your feet hip distance apart or with your feet together for more leg engagement. - Stack the balls of your feet beneath your heels. Straighten your legs by engaging your quadriceps to lift the kneecaps. - Gaze down to lengthen the back of the neck. 6. Cobra Pose Cobra, also called Bhujangasana, is a beginner-friendly backend that doesn't require the strength of Upward Facing Dog. Here's how to do Cobra: - Lie on the ground with your chest on the floor. Place your feet hip-distance apart. Bring your hands in line with your elbows and bottom ribs. - Straighten your legs by engaging your quadriceps and glutes. Press firmly through the tops of the feet to lift the kneecaps off the mat. - Lightly press through your hands. Knit your shoulder blades together and down to draw your chest forward and up. - Gaze forward to lengthen the back of the neck. 7. Warrior 1 Warrior 1, also called Virabhadrasana 1, is one of the first poses all yogis learn. It's a foundational standing posture. Here's how to do Warrior 1: - From Mountain Pose, step back with one foot. - Keep your feet hip distance apart to square your hips to the front of the mat. Stack your front shin in a straight line from knee to ankle. - Spin the back heel to the mat and angle the toes to point slightly forward and out. Root down through the feet and lift your back inner thigh to the sky. - Engage your core to lift the torso, and reach your arms to the sky with hands shoulder-distance apart. - Pull your legs energetically towards each other to find mula bandha. Gaze forward or up. 8. Warrior 2 Warrior 2, also called Virabhadrasana 2, is a very commonly performed posture that you'll practice in many different types of classes. Here's how to do Warrior 2: - From Warrior 1, maintain your stance and open your body to the side. - Change your back foot position to be in line with the back of your mat. The heel of your front foot should be in line with the arch of the back foot. - Bend your front knee directly over your ankle, bringing your front thigh parallel to the mat. To straighten the back leg, lift the inner thigh while opening the front hip. - Keeping your torso upright, engage the upper back. - Reach your arms out parallel to the mat, away from the body. Gaze forward. 9. Chair pose Chair, also called Utkatasana, is a basic standing pose that's great for improving leg strength. Here's how to do Chair Pose: - From Mountain Pose (Tadasana), bend your knees deeply and shift weight into your heels. - Try to bring your shins into a straight line from your knees to the tops of your feet. - Lift your arms to the sky with your palms facing one another and fingers spread wide. Gaze forward or up. 10. Low Lunge Low Lunge, also called Anjaneyasana, is a nice hip flexor stretch, and it's a great pose for improving your balance. Here's how to do Low Lunge: - From Mountain Pose, step back with one foot and place it on the ground behind you. Keep your feet hip-distance apart to square hips to the front of the mat. - Stack your front shin in a straight line from knee to ankle. Lower your back knee to the mat and untuck the toes. Reach your arms to the sky with hands shoulder distance apart. - Gaze forward or up.
